activities.anchor: The plan starts from two definitions
activities.caption: drag between the two properties
activities.name: perHealthCompare

before.label: Health
before.text: a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease (the WHO definition) — a property of the person.

after.label: Fitness
after.text: the ability to meet the demands of the environment — a property of a person for a task: the marathon runner fit for 42 km and unfit for a 1-rep maximum.

config.why: The relationship is positive but loose — fit-but-unhealthy (overtrained, RED-S) and healthy-but-unfit (sedentary, no disease, three flights of stairs) both exist; a good programme serves both.

activities.anchor: the standard taxonomy splits in two
activities.caption: file each component under its family
activities.name: perComponentsSort

config.prompt: File each component under its family:
config.why: Every sport demands a different weighting — and no block can maximise all of them at once, because the adaptations partially conflict (the interference effect).

activities.anchor: You cannot periodise what you cannot measure
activities.caption: pair each protocol with the component it reads
activities.name: perProtocolsMatch

config.prompt: Pair each protocol with the component it reads:
config.why: Validity asks whether the protocol captures the component in this sport's context; reliability asks for the same answer twice.

activities.anchor: an athlete's muscle glycogen store is roughly
activities.caption: estimate the carbohydrate tank
activities.name: perGlycogenEstimate

config.prompt: How big is the carbohydrate tank a hard session draws down, in grams?
config.why: 400–500 g — about 1,600–2,000 kcal, which a hard 90-minute session can meaningfully deplete; hence carbohydrate intake scaled to training load.

activities.anchor: The plan obeys a small set of principles
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the progression rules
activities.name: perOverloadSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is wrong — click it:
lines: Progressive overload: the stimulus must exceed what the body is used to — and keep growing.
Load is volume load (sets × reps × kg) or duration × intensity.
Progression is applied one variable at a time — add reps before load.
When adaptation stalls, raise every variable at once.
The 2-for-2 rule: exceeding the rep target by two, in two consecutive sessions, raises the load.
config.correction: One variable at a time — add reps before load; stall, add a back-off set, then reset load 10% and rebuild.
config.why: The programme is the progression rules, not the numbers on this week's page.

activities.anchor: The classical structure (Matveyev) nests three cycles
activities.caption: order the year's block sequence
activities.name: perMesoOrder

items: Maximal strength — lower volume, high load
config.why: Each block banks its residual effect for the next — which is why a strength block's gains are carried into a speed block rather than trained simultaneously.

config.prompt: Meta-analyses of the final-week volume cut find performance gains of about what? Place it on the scale:
config.why: Around 2–3% on average — in a final, the difference between medalling and watching; volume falls 40–60% while intensity stays.

choices.label: Under-recovery — adaptation happens during recovery, not the session

mis1.text: That is the folk trap — the staller is usually under-recovering relative to a plan copied from someone else's schedule, genetics and food budget.

rec.text: The programme's job is to schedule stress the body can absorb. What next?

choices.label: Check sleep, food budget and the copied plan's assumptions
Push through — plateaus break with grit

mis2.text: Grit without absorption is just accumulated fatigue — the adaptation never arrives.

end.text: Schedule stress the body can absorb; recovery is where adaptation happens.

config.why: The programme's job is scheduling absorbable stress — plateaus are usually under-recovery, not insufficient work.
